finalResponse:
# Second Pass

*The brief has come back to me unchanged. I'll take that as neutral — but I'd note, without pressing it, that nothing in the intervening period has narrowed which of the three gaps we're treating. So I'll assume the taxonomy is still ahead of us and offer the things I'd want ready for when it lands. These are additions, not replacements.*

---

## The contacts that arrive before anything has gone wrong

Nearly every support budget is spent downstream of a failure. But in an unfamiliar market the highest-value conversation is the one happening *before* purchase — will this fit someone built like me, what will customs add to the price, does the plug match my wall, who do I chase if it doesn't arrive. Those questions mostly don't get asked. They get resolved by abandoning the basket, silently, and we file it under conversion rather than service.

I'd staff for that deliberately: a small pre-purchase presence, reachable on the channel the market already uses, answering with candour including when the answer is *don't buy this one*. It's the cheapest trust we will ever buy, and it converts support from a cost line into something the commercial side has a reason to protect. It also generates, at no extra cost, the most accurate product-information defect list we'll ever have.

## Make the failure expensive where it was manufactured

The escalation ladder I'd delete goes upward, toward a supervisor who did not cause the problem and cannot fix its source. I'd replace it with one that goes *sideways*.

A case stuck on a broken delivery promise routes to the person who owns that carrier relationship — their inbox, their name, their week. And every contact carries a fully-loaded cost that is charged internally to the function that produced it, published monthly, unignorably. Not to punish; to make visible what is currently a free externality. Right now logistics can degrade its promise indefinitely and the invoice lands in customer service. Fix the accounting and a surprising amount of the strategy writes itself without anyone needing to be persuaded.

Some people will find this a hostile instrument. It is, mildly. That is roughly its purpose.

## Refunds that don't have to travel

Cross-border returns are frequently a piece of theatre in which we pay more in freight than the item is worth, in order to receive back something we will discount anyway. Meanwhile the customer is asked to find a printer, a box and a courier in order to be made whole — and rates the experience accordingly.

Worth modelling seriously: below a value threshold, *don't ask for it back*. Refund, and let them keep it, give it away, whatever. Above that, a local consolidation and resale partner so the goods never re-cross the border. The numbers usually work, and the second-order effect is larger than the first — a returns policy that costs the customer nothing to use is a purchase-anxiety remover on every future order, which is a merchandising asset disguised as a logistics decision.

## What does an apology cost here?

We assume remorse has a universal currency. It doesn't. Store credit reads as generosity in one market and as an insult — *you kept my money and now I must spend it with you* — in another. A discount code can imply the relationship is transactional. A telephone call from a named person can be worth more than any of them, or can read as intrusive.

Small, cheap, quietly run: four remedies, randomised across matched failures, measured on repurchase at ninety days rather than on the survey. Nobody needs to be told we're doing it. We'd learn more in a quarter than any amount of consultancy benchmarking.

## Our clock is not their clock

Support hours are usually inherited from a head-office rota and then locally "adjusted." I'd invert it — build the roster from when this market actually shops and actually complains, which tends to cluster around evenings, payday cycles, and the fortnight around whichever festival matters most here. Peak preparedness for *their* calendar, not our Black Friday. Missing a market's principal gifting season by staffing for someone else's is the sort of error nobody ever writes down.

## Hire the people who already know

Three sources I'd use before opening a conventional requisition. The competitor's former agents, who will tell us in a week what a benchmarking exercise would take a quarter to approximate. Our own most articulate complainers — the person who wrote three hundred furious, precise words has done unpaid diagnostic work and would often rather be listened to than compensated. And small distributed cells of people who already belong to the relevant communities, working part-time from wherever they are, rather than one room full of headsets. Fluid beats formal here; the market is not homogeneous and a single site will quietly flatten it.

## Presence in rooms we don't own

Our own account will always be read as advertising, whatever we put in it. The forums, groups and comment threads where this market already discusses us are not ours to control, and that is precisely their value. I'd have our people there under real names, identified, answering, occasionally conceding a point publicly.

The instinct will be to police this with an approvals process. The approvals process is what will kill it — nothing reads as more corporate than a delayed, legally-vetted reply. If we can't tolerate an individual speaking for us unsupervised, we shouldn't be in the room at all.

## An override right, with the burden reversed

The structural change I'd most want, and the one likeliest to be negotiated away: the local team can suspend any global policy for ninety days on its own authority. No business case in advance. If the centre wants it back, the centre argues for it — with evidence, afterwards.

This will be uncomfortable. It is also the only mechanism I know that reliably surfaces the policies which are being followed here purely because they were written elsewhere. Every such policy is currently generating contacts we're paying to answer.

## The people who never write

Everything above concerns customers who contacted us. The larger loss is the cohort who didn't — who received something wrong, decided it wasn't worth the effort, and never returned. They don't appear in satisfaction data at all; they appear as a slow, unattributed decay in repurchase.

I'd go and find fifty of them and simply ask. Not a survey — a conversation, in language, with someone senior enough to act on it. That's a small piece of work with an unreasonable return, and it's the sort of thing that never gets scheduled because it has no owner.

---

## What I'd resist

The service guarantee announced loudly before we can hold it. The chatbot placed in front of a human. Any initiative whose primary output is a press release. And the temptation, once some of this starts working, to tell everyone.

---

The pattern in all of the above, if it's useful to say aloud once: almost none of it is a customer service intervention. It is authority moved closer to the market, costs moved closer to their cause, and a willingness to be told something inconvenient by people whose job titles don't currently entitle them to say it.

Which returns us, gently, to the question I left open last time — and which I notice hasn't yet come back with an answer.
